prompt: For بِسْمِ, what are the visible pieces and why is a host-only gloss 'name' unsafe?
expected_answer: The token is بِـ (preposition) + host noun ٱسْمِ; the hover must preserve the bā' ('in the name of'), because a host-only 'name' drops the prepositional relation that is part of the token.
accepted_variants: bā' preposition + host اسم; 'in the name of', not 'name'
forbidden_answers: name only
the bā' is decoration
the whole token is one noun

prompt: For أَعْطَيْنَاكَ, name the pieces and the safe gloss, and why bare 'gave' fails.
expected_answer: Verb host أَعْطَيْـ + subject marker نا (we) + object pronoun كَ (you); the gloss is 'We gave you'. Bare 'gave' fails because it drops the subject 'we' and the object 'you' that the attached pieces carry.
accepted_variants: verb + نا subject + كَ object; 'We gave you'
'We gave you'; bare 'gave' drops subject and object

the كَ object pronoun can be omitted
نا is the root

concept: tanwīn-alif is not the pronoun نا
prompt: For قُرْءَانًا, why must you not split a final نا as an attached pronoun?
expected_answer: The final ـًا is tanwīn fatḥ on a carrier alif (nunation, an indefinite marker), not the attached pronoun نا. Do not split it as a pronoun; the token is one indefinite noun.
accepted_variants: ـًا is tanwīn on a carrier alif, not the pronoun نا
no clitic split; it is nunation, not 'us'
forbidden_answers: the نا is an attached pronoun 'us'
split off نا as a suffix
the alif is a separate word

prompt: For وَٱلْعَصْرِ at the start of a sūrah, why can 'and' be wrong, and what must be settled first?
expected_answer: The clause-initial وَ may be an oath particle ('by'), not the coordinating 'and'; the frame must be settled before glossing. With the oath frame the token is 'by (the) time', and the article ٱل and host ٱلْعَصْر keep their roles.
accepted_variants: oath waw 'by', not 'and', once the oath frame is set
settle oath vs conjunction before glossing وَٱلْعَصْرِ
forbidden_answers: وَ is always 'and'
ignore the oath frame
the article can vanish into the noun

concept: active-participle plural, not the entry verb

expected_answer: The token is ٱل + an active-participle plural host; it contributes 'the successful ones', not the entry infinitive 'to succeed'. A derived noun is glossed as a noun, and the plural ending must be visible.

concept: the sun/moon letter class decides the article's lam in both directions
prompt: For الْقَمَرُ, is the lam of the article ال pronounced here? Give the general rule that tells you whether the article's lam surfaces as an 'l' sound or merges into the next letter, and apply it to this word.
expected_answer: The lam is pronounced here because ق is a moon letter (outside the closed sun-letter set), so the article's lam stays audible; only when the next letter is one of the fixed sun letters does the lam assimilate instead. The rule must be checked in both directions — moon letters keep the lam, sun letters merge it — not treated as a one-way habit of just dropping the lam.
accepted_variants: ق is a moon letter, so ال keeps an audible lam; only the closed sun-letter set triggers assimilation
the lam surfaces before a moon letter and merges only before a sun letter; check both directions
forbidden_answers: the lam of the article is always silent
any letter can trigger assimilation, not just the closed sun-letter set
moon letters also double the following consonant
required_reasoning: letter after the article classified as a moon letter
closed sun-letter set treated as the trigger, not a general rule
both directions (moon keeps, sun merges) checked

concept: sun-letter assimilation is merger, not deletion, of the article's lam
prompt: For النَّهْرُ, the ن after ال carries a shadda. Has the article's lam been deleted, or has it merged into the ن? Explain what the doubled consonant actually represents.
expected_answer: The article's lam has not been deleted; it has assimilated into the following sun letter ن, and the resulting gemination (shadda) on the ن IS the surviving lam, not a separate ornament. The article's contribution is still present — it just surfaces as the doubling rather than as a separate 'l' sound.
accepted_variants: the shadda on ن is the assimilated lam, not proof the article vanished
assimilation merges the lam into the sun letter; the doubling is the lam's surviving trace
forbidden_answers: the article's lam is deleted before a sun letter
the shadda has nothing to do with the article
the host word simply has a doubled letter unrelated to ال
required_reasoning: gemination identified as the assimilated lam
assimilation described as merger, not deletion
article's contribution kept even without an audible 'l'

concept: the protective nun before the 1st-person object marks the object pronoun on a verb
prompt: For يُكْرِمُنِي, what does the نِي ending mark, and what is lost if a learner reads it the way ي is read on a noun?
expected_answer: The ending نِي is the protective nun ن plus the first-person object pronoun ي ('me'): the verb yukrimu ('he honors') takes نِي as its direct object suffix. If a learner reads the final ي the way a noun's possessive ي ('my') is read, the protective nun is ignored and the object pronoun on the verb effectively disappears from the reading — the sentence becomes an unattached fragment instead of 'he honors me.'
accepted_variants: نِي on a verb = protective nun + object pronoun 'me'; reading it as a noun's possessive ي drops the object
the object pronoun 'me' survives only if the protective nun is recognized as part of the ending, not folded away
forbidden_answers: نِي is just the possessive ي the same as on a noun
the protective nun can be ignored
the object pronoun is optional here
required_reasoning: protective nun identified as part of the object-pronoun ending
object pronoun 'me' kept, not folded into a possessive reading
verb vs noun ي-ending contrast named
